list.listitem: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a chronic, relapsing condition associated with increased morbidity and death; however, with appropriate treatment and monitoring, individuals can reach long-term remission. A

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPTF) in 2020 recommended screening for illicit drug use in adults age 18 years or older by asking questions; current evidence is insufficient to assess screening to prevent drug use in children and adolescents.
B

Management of opioid use disorder through detoxification alone is not recommended because this approach is associated with elevated risk of death from overdose and high rates of resumption of disease. A

Medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) reduces mortality over 50% doubles rates of illicit opioid free outcomes in randomized, controlled trials comparing psychosocial treatment of opioid use disorder with medication versus with placebo or no medication. A

background.definition: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is defined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) as a problematic pattern of opioid use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress. OUD was previously classified as “opioid abuse” or “opioid dependence” in DSM-IV-TR. OUD has also been referred to as "opioid addiction."

list.listitem: In the United States, 5.1 million people (1.9 percent of persons age 12 or older) were estimated in 2015 to have used heroin at some point in their lives; 329,000 (0.1 percent) reported use in the last month Heroin use in the United States has increased since 2007 (e.g., the number of past-year users increased from 373,000 to 828,000 between 2007 and 2015). There also has been an increase in heroin-related overdose deaths with 13,000 reported in 2015.

From 1999 to 2008, overdose death rates, sales, and substance use disorder treatment admissions related to prescription pain relievers increased in parallel. The overdose death rate in 2008 was nearly four times the 1999 rate; sales of prescription pain relievers in 2010 were four times those in 1999; and, the substance use disorder treatment admission rate in 2009 was six times the 1999 rate.
Overdose deaths involving opioids alone have increased dramatically in recent years to 49,000 in 2017 from 42,000 in 2016.
In 2016, 11.5 million people self-reported that they had personally misused prescription opioids during the previous year.
About 2.1 million Americans had opioid use disorder in 2016.
Contaminated drugs and inadequately sterile technique with injection drug use leads to localized and systemic infections (e.g., cellulitis, abscess, endocarditis, osteomyelitis).

Injection drug use with shared needles or syringes is associated with an increased risk of infection with a bloodborne pathogen, such as HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Hepatitis C virus infection may also occur in those who use heroin but do not inject it. Transmission has been associated with tattooing and sharing of straws for intranasal insufflation.
Opioid use disorder is associated with increased mortality compared with the general population secondary to infection, overdose, and trauma.
Opioid use disorder is considered a biopsychosocial disease. Pharmacological, social, genetic, and psychodynamic factors interact to influence risky use behaviors.
Social milieu encourages (or discourages) drug use, and psychological factors such as anxiety and depression play a significant role.
Family history and a personal history of other substance use are important risk factors.

Physiological opioid dependence occurs when the frequent and repeated use of opioids leads to structural changes in the brain such that normal brain function requires the presence of exogenous opioids.
Physiological changes to the brain result in a hypersensitization of the brain’s reward system so that the patient experiences cravings and withdrawal in the absence of opioids.
Structural changes also occur in neuronal circuits involved in learning and memory, motivation and drive, and inhibitory control.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPTF) in 2020 recommended screening for illicit drug use in adults age 18 years or older; current evidence is insufficient to assess screening to prevent drug use in children and adolescents.
B
Effective prevention programs emphasize deterrent factors such as family cohesion, self-esteem, life skills training, motivational interviewing, family interventions, and community support.13, 14 B

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPTF) in 2020 recommended screening for illicit drug use in adults age 18 years or older using questions; current evidence is insufficient to assess screening in adolescents.

Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment (SBIRT) is an evidence-based practice used to identify, reduce, and prevent problematic use, misuse and substance use disorder identification for persons consuming alcohol and illicit drugs. There is substantial research on the effectiveness of SBIRT in reducing risky alcohol consumption. However, the evidence for the effectiveness of SBIRT in reducing risky drug use, although promising, is still accumulating.

The CAGE-AID (CAGE questions Adapted to Include Drugs) is a brief screening tool that asks: Have you ever felt that you ought to Cut down on your drinking or drug use? Have people Annoyed you by criticizing your drinking or drug use? Have you ever felt bad or Guilty about your drinking or drug use? Have you ever had a drink or used drugs first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or to get rid of a hangover (Eye opener)? One or more positive answers indicates a positive screen (sensitivity 0.79 and specificity 0.77) and need for further evaluation.

The Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST) was developed in 1982 and is a 28-item self-report scale. The DAST has exhibited valid psychometric properties and has been found to be a sensitive screening instrument for the abuse of drugs other than alcohol.
Patients with a family history of substance use disorder are at increased risk (30%-40%); consider screening.
Effective prevention programs emphasize deterrent factors such as family cohesion, self-esteem, life skills training, and community support.
Motivational interviewing and family interventions may be effective for preventing drug use in young people.
Skills-based programs in schools appear to prevent early stage drug use in children.

The 2016 CDC guidelines for prescribing opiates for chronic pain suggests use of nonpharmacologic therapies (e.g., exercise), and nonopioid pain medications, discussing risks of long-term opioid use, using the lowest effective dose with frequent and regular re-evaluation, and using risk mitigation tools.
The USPSTF concluded that there was insufficient evidence to recommend counseling to prevent illicit drug use in children and young adults (I statement).
A study found that increasing amounts of substance use and use by their parents when teens are 16 years old predicts opioid use disorder at 25 years of age.
Having a consistent usual prescriber (i.e., family physician) pre-operatively and returning to that provider post-operatively is associated with a lower likelihood of developing opioid use disorder.

Policy measures associated with decreased opioid use disorder include well designed and implemented prescription drug monitoring programs, pill-mill laws, pain clinic regulations, provider education, and marijuana laws.

A systematic review of 14 cohort studies concluded that persistent opioid use is more likely with older age, having a physical comorbidity, having a past or current substance use disorder, receiving prescriptions lasting more than 7 days, and receiving higher morphine equivalents daily.

Educational strategies, which aim to raise awareness and understanding about the dangers of prescription drug overdoses, how to recognize when an individual is at risk for overdose, how to recognize when an overdose is occurring, how to appropriately respond to an overdose, and the laws relevant to overdoses (i.e., Good Samaritan Laws).

Tracking and monitoring strategies, which may involve expanding, improving, or mandating use of Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) in order to prevent individuals from receiving medically unnecessary prescriptions, that may be misused and cause overdose.
Supply reduction strategies, which limit access to commonly misused prescription drugs in order to reduce doctor-shopping behavior and the amount of controlled drugs in circulation.
Harm reduction strategies including naloxone distribution, overdose education and safe syringe exchange programs.

A meta-analysis concluded that using mindfulness meditation, hypnosis, therapeutic suggestion, and cognitive behavioral therapy, in addition to opioid treatment of either acute or chronic pain, provides an additional benefit to patients by reducing pain scores. Some of these interventions will decrease either the duration or amount of opioid needed.
Patients should be diagnosed with opioid use disorder based on diagnostic criteria from the DSM-5 with the severity of the disorder described as mild, moderate, or severe. C

There are several physical and mental health disorders that may present with signs and symptoms consistent with opioid use disorder requiring a history, physical, and laboratory testing. These disorders may include sedative-hypnotic toxicity, anxiety disorders, personality disorders, depression and bipolar disorder. C

listitem.strong: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition defines opioid use disorder as two or more of the following within a 12-month period:

list.listitem: Using larger amounts of opioids or over a longer period than was intended.
Persistent desire to cut down or unsuccessful efforts to control use.
Great deal of time spent obtaining, using, or recovering from use.
Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use substance.
Failure to fulfill major role obligations at work, school, or home due to recurrent opioid use.
Continued use despite recurrent or persistent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by opioid use.
Giving up or reducing social, occupational, or recreational activities due to opioid use.
Recurrent opioid use in physically hazardous situations.
Continued opioid use despite physical or psychological problems caused or exacerbated by its use.
Tolerance (marked increase in amount; marked decrease in effect).

Withdrawal syndrome as manifested by cessation of opioids or use of opioids (or a closely related substance) to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms. Tolerance and withdrawal criteria alone are not sufficient to make the diagnosis (e.g., taking opioids solely under appropriate medical supervision).
Severity of opioid use disorder is categorized as mild (presence of 2-3 symptoms), moderate (4-5 symptoms), or severe (6 or more symptoms).
Assess the patient for suicidality. Take a list of the substances and amounts used, and route of administration (oral, intranasal, IV, subcutaneous "skin popping", smoking).

Ask about previous treatments for substance use disorder and/or 12-step involvement with durations of successful treatment, as well as factors and circumstances contributing to disease resumption or worsening.
Inquire about infection with HIV, hepatitis, abscesses, endocarditis, and any history of sexual abuse or domestic violence.

Examine eyes for pupils: miosis (intoxication), mydriasis (withdrawal), ptosis (intoxication), Roth spots (endocarditis); nasal septal erosions or perforations (e.g., snorting crushed OxyContin tablets); skin for sweating, piloerection (withdrawal), splinter hemorrhages (endocarditis), needle marks, "tracks" phlebitis, abscesses; heart for murmur (endocarditis); and abdomen for decreased bowel sounds (intoxication) or hyperactive (withdrawal), or palpable liver (hepatitis).

Symptoms and signs of opiate withdrawal are anxiety, restlessness, yawning, insomnia, stomach cramps, diarrhea, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, muscle spasms ("kicking the habit"), diaphoresis, night sweats, tachycardia, hypertension, piloerection ("cold turkey"), mydriasis, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Short half-life opiates (morphine, hydrocodone, oxycodone, heroin, etc.) have earlier peak symptoms (3-5 days) and briefer duration of symptoms (7-10 days), whereas symptoms peak later (7-10 days) and last longer (2-4 weeks) with longer half-life opiates (methadone or buprenorphine).

A decreased respiratory rate less than 12 is a highly sensitive indicator for opiate overdose and is a characteristic opiate effect. A depressed level of consciousness, miosis, ptosis, decreased tidal volume, and hypotension may also occur in overdoses with other substances.

listitem.strong: Perform laboratory testing based on clinical circumstances:

list.listitem: Test urine for opioids, alcohol (and its metabolite ethyl glucuronide), and other drugs, such as benzodiazepines. Rapid urine drug screens, usually immunoassays, may not detect some opiates, particularly synthetics such as buprenorphine, methadone or fentanyl. Immunoassays are subject to false positives and false negatives and should be confirmed by another method before making clinical decisions. Gas chromatography with mass spectroscopy is precise but expensive and may take several days for results. Drug screen results are suggestive at best. NOTE: Presence of opioids is not sufficient to diagnose opioid use disorder, and an absence of opioids does not rule out opioid use disorder.
Obtain a complete blood count (especially if any signs of bacterial infection such as endocarditis).
Assess for hepatitis B/C and HIV for those who use inject drugs.
Offer hepatitis A and B vaccination for patients who inject drugs and have negative hepatitis serology.
Offer PrEP as appropriate for patients who are at risk of HIV.
Consider testing for syphilis and tuberculosis if indicated.
Assess liver and kidney function with liver enzymes, serum bilirubin, and serum creatinine blood tests.
Patients should be assessed for opioid use disorder if they screen positive for opioid misuse, disclose opioid misuse, or exhibit signs or symptoms of opioid misuse.
The patient should be assessed and treated for co-occurring medical or mental disorders.
Motivational brief interventions promote safer behavior and foster effective treatment engagement.
The provider should provide overdose education and prescribe or otherwise instruct the patient on how to obtain naloxone.
Patients who inject drugs should be instructed on how to access sterile injecting equipment.
Patients with opioid use disorder should be referred for treatment with medication for opioid use disorder (buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone).

Medication for addiction treatment of opioid use disorder at least doubles rates of illicit opioid free outcomes in randomized, controlled trials comparing psychosocial treatment of opioid use disorder with medication versus with placebo or no medication. A
Medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) cuts mortality in half. A
Best outcomes result from MOUD treatment for at least 3 months. A

Clinical practice guidelines encourage the use of buprenorphine and methadone as MOUD. Both medications were given a level A rating, indicating that a strong level of evidence was found and that the intervention benefits outweighed harms. Factors including availability of methadone facilities, a patient's ability to meet the requirements associated with a treatment program, the safety profiles of buprenorphine and methadone, and patient preference should be considered when helping patients determine which treatment option best fits their needs.

A systematic review found that the optimal methadone dosage is between 60 and 100 mg/day. Methadone maintenance may only be administered by registered opioid treatment programs (methadone clinics), and to prescribe buprenorphine for opiate use disorder the prescriber must obtain a waiver from the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in the United States.

Treatment with either methadone or buprenorphine reduces mortality approximately 50% as shown in a 2017 meta -analysis. These findings were confirmed by a 2018 study of patients treated for overdose in the emergency room, as well as by a second meta-analysis.
In the appropriately supervised setting, supervised heroin use has been shown to add slight benefit to methadone alone in patients who have failed other medical treatment.
Long term buprenorphine treatment initiated during hospitalization with a link to an outpatient program improves opioid use and increases engagement.

In a systematic review that evaluated functional outcomes, the quality of evidence for most functional outcomes was rated low or very low. In sum, weaknesses in the body of evidence prevent strong conclusions about the effects of MOUD on functional outcomes. Rigorous studies of functional effects would strengthen the body of literature.

Oral naltrexone: The conclusion of a Cochrane review states that studies conducted have not allowed an adequate evaluation of oral naltrexone treatment in the field of opioid use disorder. Consequently, longitudinal therapy with oral naltrexone cannot yet be considered a treatment which has been scientifically proved to be superior to other kinds of treatment. Oral naltrexone treatment is limited by poor patient adherence.

Long-acting naltrexone: Extended-release injectable naltrexone is an efficacious treatment for opioid use disorder that is useful for patients who have contraindications to, or who failed pharmacotherapy with buprenorphine and methadone; patients confined to drug-free environments such as prison or inpatient rehabilitation; patients living in areas where agonist treatment is not available; individuals who are highly motivated and are willing to taper off their current agonist therapy; or patients who simply do not want to be treated with an agonist. Because it is FDA-approved for the treatment of alcohol use disorder, it may be well suited for patients with co-occurring opioid and alcohol use disorders.
Long-acting naltrexone: Extended-release injectable naltrexone blocks the effects of opiates and the risk of overdose. It also reduces craving for opiates.
There is preliminary evidence from a small study with 42 abstinent patients that oral cannabidiol (CBD) may reduce craving and anxiety more than placebo.

A Cochrane review showed no significant differences between different psychosocial interventions; however, the studies were difficult to compare due to small individual sample sizes and variability in protocols.
Short-acting opioids allow flexible titration to withdrawal symptoms but require frequent administration and are best used in a controlled environment (inpatient/residential treatment).
Long-acting opioids such as methadone and buprenorphine can be administered once daily and are suited well to outpatient treatment.
Buprenorphine and methadone are equally effective in treating opioid withdrawal symptoms.
Anesthesia or heavy sedation for rapid opioid withdrawal using opioid antagonists is not recommended because of the risk for serious and potentially fatal complications.

Alpha-adrenergic medications like clonidine (0.1-0.3 mg three times daily) and lofexidine decrease opioid withdrawal symptoms and improve completion of treatment. Concerns include hypotension, rebound hypertension when discontinued, sedation, and some misuse potential.

Insomnia can be treated with the sedating antidepressant trazodone, intestinal cramping is reduced with anticholinergic medications (e.g., dicyclomine), and muscle spasms are reduced with skeletal muscle relaxants (e.g., cyclobenzaprine). However, carisoprodol should be avoided because of its significant risk of misuse.

Naloxone is available in most states without prescription and may be administered by a layperson intranasally (2 or 4 mg) or intramuscularly via autoinjector (2 mg) along with instructions to call emergency services when administered.

Naloxone should be administered in increments of 0.05 mg IV, repeated every 2 to 3 minutes until adequate respirations are restored. Ventilation should be assessed and supported during administration of naloxone. Patients who are apneic or in cardiac arrest should receive naloxone 0.4 mg IV, or greater. If no effect is seen after 5 mg of naloxone, other diagnoses should be considered.
Rapid reversal of opioid effects is a suspected cause of cardiac arrhythmia, pulmonary edema, and mortality.

Substance use disorders in adolescents are common in those with co-morbid psychiatric illness and/or who experience peer or family pressures or exposure to the use of substances. A comprehensive care plan including thorough assessment, case management, family therapy which consider culture and gender are critical for adolescent substance use care. Therapy in group settings should be conducted by trained counselors or therapists as some group members may reinforce drug use and distract from the purpose of the therapy. Buprenorphine is FDA approved for those 18 and older, but has been studied and is suggested to be efficacious in individuals as young as 16.

There is a dearth of empirical research on the optimal psychosocial interventions to use with MOUD. A systematic review evaluated 3 reviews and 27 publications of empirical studies on this topic. The most widely studied psychosocial interventions in this review examined in conjunction with MOUD were contingency management and cognitive behavioral therapy, with the majority in combination with methadone treatment. The results generally support the efficacy of providing psychosocial interventions in combination with MOUD, although the incremental utility varied across studies, outcomes, medications, and interventions.
Group therapy is a common feature of abstinence-based treatment, but the evidence base is poor with no clear support for one type of treatment over another.

Groups may be psychoeducational, interpersonal-process, skill training (stress management, relapse prevention, and meditation/guided imagery), 12-step support groups (e.g., Narcotics Anonymous), or special population groups based on gender, sexual orientation, occupation, and other factors.

12-step support groups increase abstinence and have 3 year outcomes similar to accepted therapies (cognitive behavioral therapy and motivational enhancement therapy). A recent Cochrane review concluded that 12-step programs are more effective than established treatments (e.g., CBT) for abstinence from alcohol. A pooled data analysis demonstrated that 12-step programs also reduce drug use.

Family involvement in treatment provides strong support for patient recovery; and family members also benefit. The concept of ‘‘family’’ should be expanded to include members of the patient’s social network (as defined by the patient), including significant others, clergy, employers, and case managers.

A randomized trial with 400 adults found that a patient navigator focused on case management, advocacy, and motivational support reduced the likelihood of readmission compared with treatment as usual (6 vs 8.1 admissions per 1000 person-days, p = 0.02).
Patients having failed prior attempts at outpatient treatment, dual diagnoses with a mental health disorder, or suicidality should be managed in an inpatient or residential treatment program.
HIV: people who inject drugs (PWID) account for 6% of HIV infections. There has been a 48% decrease in HIV diagnosis in PWID between 2008 and 2014.
Hepatitis B (HBV): In a study of southern Appalachia (KY, TN, WV) the incidence of HBV has increased 114% between 2009 and 2013.

Hepatitis C (HCV): In a study of southern Appalachia (KY, TN, VA, WV) between 2006 and 2012 there was a 364% increase in cases of HCV and 73% of cases of HCV were in PWID. During the same period there was a 21% increase in treatment admissions for opioid use disorder.

Pain treatment may require large opioid doses in opioid-dependent patients who are actively using opioids. After detoxification, tolerance will be absent but will return rapidly (few days), requiring increasing opioid doses to maintain pain control.
The DEA permits physicians to dispense (but not prescribe) opiates to treat acute opiate withdrawal. This is limited to 72 hours (3 daily doses).

Opioid use disorder is a chronic disease, with high relapse rates in untreated patients. With effective treatment, relapse rates are similar to those in other well-characterized chronic medical illnesses, such as diabetes, hypertension, and asthma. B
The treatment of opioid use disorder involves modifying deeply ingrained behaviors; resumption of opioid use does not equal treatment failure. C

With each resumption of opioid use, the patient and healthcare providers need to evaluate whether to reinstate treatment, adjust current treatment, or find alternative treatment based on the biopsychosocial model. C

A systematic review identified only 7 studies with between 10 and 10,372 of chronic use of opioids for non-malignant pain in the elderly. There were no RCTs. They found that chronic use improved sleep quality in patients with osteoarthritis, but not function, and a range of improvements in pain. Overall the quality and amount of evidence was inadequate to draw firm conclusions.
Many of the medical risks associated with opioid use disorder are similar for both pregnant and nonpregnant women; however, opioid use disorder carries obstetrical risks for pregnant women.
Several obstetrical complications have been associated with opioid use in pregnancy, including preeclampsia, miscarriage, premature delivery, fetal growth restriction, and fetal death.

A systematic review evaluating detoxification during pregnancy concluded evidence does not support detoxification as a recommended treatment intervention as a result of low detoxification completion rates, high rates of use afterward, and limited data regarding the effect of detoxification on maternal and neonatal outcomes beyond delivery.
Pregnant women with opioid use disorder should be treated with opioid agonist treatment, especially as a return to opioid use should be expected during pregnancy.

Methadone has been the accepted standard of care for use during pregnancy. However, buprenorphine is considered a first-line treatment option. There are no significant differences in overall rates of neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) among infants exposed to buprenorphine and those exposed to methadone and buprenorphine reduces the severity of NAS.
Buprenorphine monoproduct may be used in pregnant women. There is insufficient evidence to recommend the combination buprenorphine/naloxone formulation, though there is evidence of safety.
Buprenorphine (a partial agonist) can impede opiate analgesia at time of vaginal delivery or cesarean section.
Naltrexone is not recommended to be initiated during pregnancy because of risk of precipitating opioid withdrawal.

Breastfeeding while mothers are continued on methadone or buprenorphine is encouraged as it may decrease symptoms of neonatal abstinence and provide known benefits of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding is not recommended if the mother has Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), has relapsed, or other contraindications are identified.
Pharmacologic therapy is needed in up to 80% of opioid exposed infants who cannot be managed with supportive care alone.

The American Academy of Pediatrics and Cochrane review support opioid replacement therapy (e.g., preservative free neonatal morphine solution, methadone) as the primary pharmacologic treatment for infants with moderate-to-severe NAS.
